core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Infectious Mononucleosis (EBV) is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.
Standard management emphasizes Plan for Infectious Mononucleosis: Symptomatic care, avoid contact sports (splenic rupture risk), adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: severe sore throat, high fever, and huge neck lymph nodes

Key HPI features: A 41-year-old male presents to the clinic with severe sore throat, high fever, and huge neck lymph nodes. The patient states the symptoms started recently and have been gradually worsening, accompanied by generalized fatigue.

Objective/Exam findings: Vitals: Temp 38.9C, HR 92, BP 118/74. Bilateral posterior cervical lymphadenopathy, tonsillar exudates with palatal petechiae, mild splenomegaly on abdominal palpation. Heterophile antibody (Monospot) test positive; CBC shows lymphocytosis with >10% atypical lymphocytes.
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Infectious Mononucleosis (EBV).
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Streptococcal pharyngitis without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Severe abdominal pain — could indicate splenic enlargement or rupture risk.
management_principles: Plan for Infectious Mononucleosis: Symptomatic care, avoid contact sports (splenic rupture risk)
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

reference_soap.subjective:
Chief Complaint: severe sore throat, high fever, and huge neck lymph nodes

A 41-year-old male presents to the clinic with severe sore throat, high fever, and huge neck lymph nodes. The patient states the symptoms started recently and have been gradually worsening, accompanied by generalized fatigue.
reference_soap.objective: Vitals: Temp 38.9C, HR 92, BP 118/74. Bilateral posterior cervical lymphadenopathy, tonsillar exudates with palatal petechiae, mild splenomegaly on abdominal palpation. Heterophile antibody (Monospot) test positive; CBC shows lymphocytosis with >10% atypical lymphocytes.
reference_soap.assessment: Infectious Mononucleosis (EBV), confirmed by positive heterophile antibody testing and atypical lymphocytosis; mild splenomegaly noted, warranting contact/sport precautions.
reference_soap.plan: Plan for Infectious Mononucleosis: Symptomatic care, avoid contact sports (splenic rupture risk). Consult specialist if symptoms worsen. Counsel patient.
